item.text: {"text":"Direct precedent: Zhou et al., [Is Contrastive Learning Necessary?](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.11136v1), train a shared recommender directly on augmented sequences, distinguishing target-preserving transformations such as cropping from sliding windows that introduce different prediction targets. Crop and slide-window often match or outperform contrastive methods; combining slide-window with crop can reduce performance. Experiments use SASRec, so they support supervised augmentation generally, not a demonstrated NextItNet-specific full-prefix/recent-suffix auxiliary cross-entropy objective. The exact paired suffix formulation remains an experimental hypothesis.\n\n[NextItNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163) uses autoregressive supervision and stacked causal dilated convolutions. Architectural deduction: for stride-one layers, the maximum receptive-field span is R = 1 + Σₗ(kₗ−1)dₗ, counting every convolution along the deepest path. A recent suffix retaining all input positions that can influence the final output removes no available evidence; with aligned positions, local normalization, identical padding semantics and dropout disabled, predictions should coincide. Shorter suffixes can remove accessible evidence and provide meaningful context truncation. Global pooling or sequence-wide normalization would invalidate that equivalence. Useful ablations: baseline versus duplicate-full-prefix auxiliary loss versus suffix auxiliary loss, with matched optimization budget; sweep suffix lengths below and above R. Use one shared NextItNet and output head, retain the same next-item target, and read the final nonpadding position in left-padded inputs."}
